summary: Specifies Post Office Protocol version 3, which lets a client fetch email from a server. It is a revision of RFC 1460. It has been replaced by RFC 1939.

plainLanguage.summary: Your mail waits at a post office, and this lets your computer go pick it up.

subtitle: How a small computer fetches its waiting email from a server, one session at a time.

tldr.problem: Small workstations often cannot run a full mail transport system or stay connected all day, but their users still want to manage mail.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection to port 110, authenticates with USER and PASS or the APOP command, then lists, retrieves and marks messages for deletion in a simple command and response session.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1725 was a revision of RFC 1460 and became an Internet Standard, but it was obsoleted by RFC 1939.

today: RFC 1725 is obsoleted by RFC 1939, so that is the RFC to read for the current POP3 definition. It was a revision of RFC 1460, which it obsoletes.

sections.title: Why POP3 Exists
sections.content:
Some nodes cannot keep an SMTP server and local delivery system running, because they lack cycles or disk space or because they are not connected to the network all the time. A node that can run a mail transport system offers a maildrop service to them. The Post Office Protocol, Version 3 (POP3) lets a workstation dynamically access its maildrop on a server host, usually to retrieve mail the server is holding for it.

The RFC does not specify how a client sends mail. It only suggests that the client uses SMTP to a relay host, which could be the POP3 server host. This memo is a revision of RFC 1460. Among its changes, it removes the LAST command, permits an inactivity autologout timer, adds the optional UIDL command, and adds warnings about APOP shared secret length and in the security section.
sections.plainLanguage: Little computers cannot always stay online to catch mail. A bigger computer holds it for them, and POP3 is how they collect it.

sections.title: Basic Operation and Session States
sections.content:
The server listens on TCP port 110. After the connection opens, the server sends a greeting and the two sides exchange commands and responses until the connection closes. A command is a keyword of three or four characters, possibly followed by arguments of up to 40 characters, ending in CRLF. A response starts with +OK or -ERR.

Multi-line responses end with a line holding only a period, and any data line that starts with a period gets an extra period added (byte-stuffing).

A session moves through three states. In AUTHORIZATION the client identifies itself. After a successful login, the server locks the maildrop and the session enters TRANSACTION. When the client sends QUIT, the session enters UPDATE, where the server removes messages marked as deleted, releases its resources and closes the connection.

A server MAY have an inactivity autologout timer of at least 10 minutes. If it fires, the session does not enter UPDATE and no messages are removed. The same is true for any session that ends without a client QUIT.
sections.plainLanguage: A visit has three parts: show your ID at the door, pick up and sort your letters, and then leave while the clerk throws away the ones you marked.

sections.title: Authorization and Transaction Commands
sections.content:
In AUTHORIZATION, the client sends USER name followed by PASS string. If login works, the server takes an exclusive-access lock on the maildrop and numbers the messages from 1, noting each size in octets. If the maildrop cannot be opened, the server answers -ERR and may close the connection.

In TRANSACTION the minimal commands are:

  • STAT returns the message count and total size.
  • LIST [msg] returns a scan listing of message number and exact size, for one or all messages.
  • RETR msg sends the whole message.
  • DELE msg only marks a message as deleted. The server removes it at UPDATE.
  • NOOP does nothing but reply positively.
  • RSET unmarks any deleted messages.

Messages marked as deleted are not counted or listed, and referring to one gives an error. The RFC STRONGLY discourages putting extra information in STAT and LIST lines, and instead encourages the optional commands, so that intelligence sits in the client.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask how many letters there are, read one, mark one for the trash, or change your mind about the trash. Nothing is thrown away until you leave.

sections.title: Optional Commands: TOP, UIDL and APOP
sections.content:
TOP msg n returns the message headers, a blank line and the first n lines of the body, or the whole message if it is shorter. UIDL [msg] returns a unique-id for each message, an arbitrary server-chosen string of characters in the range 0x21 to 0x7E that persists across sessions and should not be reused in that maildrop.

APOP name digest avoids sending a password in the clear. The server includes a unique timestamp in its greeting, such as <1896.697170952@dbc.mtview.ca.us>. The client computes an MD5 digest of the timestamp followed by a shared secret and sends the 16-octet result in lowercase hexadecimal. A correct digest moves the session to TRANSACTION. Otherwise the session stays in AUTHORIZATION. Shared secrets should be long strings.
sections.plainLanguage: TOP lets you peek at the start of a letter. UIDL gives each letter a permanent tag. APOP proves who you are using a secret code mixed with a fresh number, so the password never travels.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it is only conjectured that APOP provides origin identification and replay protection. A server that supports both PASS and APOP must not allow both methods for the same user, so a given USER name uses one or the other.

It also notes that a longer shared secret is harder to derive, that answering -ERR to USER gives attackers clues about valid names, that PASS sends passwords in the clear, and that RETR and TOP send mail in the clear. Otherwise security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret-code login is better than sending a plain password, but the RFC is honest that it is only believed to be safe, and the mail itself is not hidden from people listening in.
